en.clue: The movable frame that holds a shark's teeth
en.fact: A shark's jaw is loosely attached to its skull, so it can swing forward when biting.

en.clue: Body part you see with; you have two of them

en.clue: Animal with fins and gills that spends its whole life in water

en.clue: Colorful ridge of coral just under the surface of the sea

en.clue: Whiskered ocean swimmer that barks and rests on rocks

en.clue: Speedy ocean fish often packed in cans for sandwiches
en.fact: Mako sharks and tuna both keep their muscles warmer than the water around them.

en.clue: Ocean animal with ten limbs that sprays ink to escape

en.clue: Giant brown seaweed that grows in underwater forests

en.clue: Strong metal bars that protect divers watching big sharks

en.clue: What scuba swimmers do to go down deep underwater

en.clue: Move through water by kicking or sweeping fins

en.clue: Far down below the surface; the opposite of shallow

en.clue: White crystals that make the sea taste yucky
en.fact: Bull sharks can live in salty sea water and in fresh river water.

en.clue: An animal that gets hunted and eaten by another

en.clue: Sour yellow citrus fruit used in a sweet summer drink

en.clue: Color of a clear sky; a slim shark is named for it

en.clue: Tiny grains of rock that cover a beach
en.fact: Sand tiger sharks gulp air at the surface so they can float in place.

en.clue: Scientists clip this onto a shark's fin to follow its travels

en.clue: Black-and-white striped animal of the African grasslands, like a horse

en.clue: Shine softly in the dark, like a night-light

en.clue: Gadget that uses sound echoes to find things underwater

en.clue: Flat ocean fish that flaps its fins like wings; shark's cousin
en.fact: Rays and sharks are cousins, and both have skeletons made of cartilage.

en.clue: Pointy nose of a pig, a dog, or a shark
en.fact: A sawshark's long snout has two whisker-like feelers that help it find food in sand.

en.clue: Big oily organ inside a shark that helps it float
en.fact: Oil is lighter than water, so an oily liver helps keep a shark from sinking.

en.clue: Wooden stick swung in baseball to hit the ball
en.fact: A thresher shark swings its long tail like one to stun small fish.

en.clue: Small flying robot with spinning propellers, steered from the ground
en.fact: Beach lifeguards and scientists use them to spot sharks from the sky.

en.clue: How fast something moves, such as miles per hour
en.fact: A shortfin mako can swim faster than 30 miles an hour.

en.clue: Daily rise and fall of seawater at the beach
en.fact: The Moon's pull makes the ocean rise and fall along the shore.

en.clue: Spotted big cat of Africa; one small shark wears its pattern
en.fact: Leopard sharks swim in big groups in shallow bays, and they are not dangerous to people.

en.clue: Collar-like gill edges give this eel-shaped deep-sea shark its name
en.fact: A frilled shark has about 300 tiny three-pointed teeth, and it looks like an eel.

en.clue: Underwater ridge of loose grains piled up near the shore
en.fact: Sandbar sharks have a very tall first fin, and their babies grow up in shallow bays.

en.clue: Bag inside your belly where swallowed food goes
en.fact: Some sharks can flip their stomach inside out to clean it.

en.clue: Shape of a curly staircase or a snail's shell
en.fact: Inside a shark's short intestine is a corkscrew twist that gives food more surface to soak into.

en.clue: The sense you use your ears for
en.fact: Sharks can hear low sounds, like a flapping fish, from very far away.

en.clue: Gadget that snaps photos or video
en.fact: Scientists clip tiny ones to sharks to see what a day in their life looks like.

en.clue: One kind of living thing, such as a type of bird
en.fact: There are more than 500 species of sharks, and the smallest is shorter than a ruler.

en.clue: Pink fish that swims upstream to lay its eggs
en.fact: Salmon sharks live in cold northern seas but keep their bodies warmer than the water.

en.clue: Sea animal with eight arms that squirts a cloud of ink
en.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.

en.clue: Hard-shelled sea animal with two big claws, often boiled for dinner
en.fact: Nurse sharks can crunch hard-shelled food like lobsters and crabs.

en.clue: Shelled reptile that can swim in the sea
en.fact: Tiger sharks have strong jaws that can crack open a sea turtle's shell.

en.clue: Playful, smart sea mammal that clicks and whistles
en.fact: Dolphins breathe air at the surface, but sharks breathe underwater with gills.

en.clue: Calm, shallow water almost walled in by land or a reef
en.fact: Many young reef sharks grow up in the calm, shallow water of lagoons.

en.clue: Where a river meets the sea and fresh and salt water mix
en.fact: Bull sharks can swim into estuaries and even far up rivers.

en.clue: Safe shallow spot where young sharks grow; also a room for babies
en.fact: Young sharks stay in calm shallow places where big hungry animals rarely go.

en.clue: Breathing tube for swimming with your face in the water
en.fact: Snorkelers can swim beside whale sharks, which are the biggest fish in the sea.

en.clue: Not deep; water that barely covers your knees
en.fact: Many baby sharks grow up in this kind of water, away from big predators.

en.clue: Repeating design, such as spots or stripes
en.fact: Every whale shark has its own spot pattern, like a fingerprint.

en.clue: Gas in air and water that animals need to breathe
en.fact: Water holds far less of it than air does, so gills have to work hard.

en.clue: In baseball, three of these and the batter is out
en.fact: A thresher shark's tail can be as long as the rest of its body.

en.clue: Soft and kind, not rough
en.fact: Whale sharks and basking sharks are gentle giants that eat tiny food.

en.clue: Athlete who races in a pool
en.fact: Some racing swimsuits were designed to copy the tiny ridges on shark skin.

en.clue: Staying steady without falling over
en.fact: Sharks have tiny ear openings behind their eyes that help them hear and keep their balance.

en.clue: Soft covering for a living room floor
en.fact: Carpet sharks like wobbegongs lie flat on the sea floor and look like rocks.

en.clue: Shiny glass that shows your reflection
en.fact: A shark's eye has a mirror-like layer that helps it see in dim water.

en.clue: Your brain's ability to keep things from the past
en.fact: Sharks in tests have learned tasks and still remembered them weeks later.

en.clue: Freezing ocean and ice region around the North Pole
en.fact: Greenland sharks swim in near-freezing water and grow very slowly.

en.clue: How heavy something is, measured on a scale
en.fact: A whale shark weighs more than a full-grown elephant.

en.clue: Thin metal pin used for sewing, with a hole at one end
en.fact: A mako's teeth are long and thin like needles, perfect for catching slippery fish.

en.clue: Soft, holey thing for scrubbing, once a sea animal
en.fact: A sponge is an animal, even though it never moves from its spot.

en.clue: Black-and-white bird that cannot fly but swims fast
en.fact: Penguins use their wings as flippers to zoom through the water.

en.clue: Huge icy island near Canada, name of a shark that lives centuries
en.fact: Greenland sharks swim slowly in freezing water and may live for hundreds of years.

en.clue: Shark whose fin tips look dipped in dark ink
en.fact: Blacktip sharks can leap out of the water and spin while hunting fish.

en.clue: Open-ocean shark with bright pale tips on its fins
en.fact: Oceanic whitetip sharks cruise far from land, with long, rounded fins.

en.clue: Shark with a toothed snout like a carpenter's tool
en.fact: Sawsharks look like sawfish, but they are true sharks and are much smaller.

en.clue: Tiny tooth-shaped scale; thousands cover a shark's skin
en.fact: Denticles point backward, which helps water flow smoothly past a swimming shark.

en.clue: Boat that travels deep under the water
en.fact: Scientists use small research subs to film deep-sea sharks in the dark.

en.clue: Machine that circles Earth high above in space
en.fact: Some shark tags send signals to one whenever the shark's fin breaks the surface.

en.clue: Flat sea fish with a whip-like tail that hides in sand
en.fact: Stingrays have their eyes on top of their bodies and their mouths underneath.

en.clue: Tree whose tangled roots grow in salty shallow water
en.fact: Baby lemon sharks hide among the roots of these trees to stay safe.

en.clue: Small hammerhead cousin with a rounded, shovel-shaped head
en.fact: Unlike most sharks, bonnetheads eat lots of seagrass and can digest part of it.

en.clue: Underwater plant that grows in green meadows on the sandy sea floor
en.fact: It is a flowering plant that lives underwater, and sea turtles love to eat it.

en.clue: Building with big tanks where you can watch fish and sea animals
en.fact: Some have glass tunnels where visitors walk right under swimming sharks.

en.clue: Colors and patterns that help an animal blend in
en.fact: A wobbegong's fringed skin flaps make it nearly invisible on the sea floor.

en.clue: What you see in a room with all the lights off
en.fact: Below about 3,000 feet, sunlight never reaches the ocean, so deep-sea sharks live in the dark.

en.clue: Squeezing force of deep water on everything in it
en.fact: Deep-sea pressure can shrink a foam cup to a tiny size, yet sharks live there.

en.clue: Edged with tiny sharp points, like a steak knife
en.fact: Tiger shark and great white teeth are like this, which helps them slice tough food.

en.clue: Shape with three straight sides and three corners
en.fact: A great white's teeth are shaped like tall triangles with sawlike edges.

en.clue: All the bones in a body, standing together
en.fact: Because shark skeletons are made of soft cartilage, mostly their teeth survive as fossils.

en.clue: Person who studies nature by asking questions and running experiments
en.fact: Scientists can tell the age of some sharks by counting rings in their backbones, like tree rings.

en.clue: Hot, wet climate near the equator
en.fact: Many kinds of sharks prefer warm tropical seas, where lots of fish live.

en.clue: Floaty sea animal with stinging tentacles and no brain
en.fact: Jellyfish have been drifting in the sea for longer than sharks have.

en.clue: Least big of all; the opposite of largest
en.fact: The dwarf lanternshark is one of the smallest sharks, shorter than a ruler, and it glows.

en.clue: Sunken boat resting on the sea floor
en.fact: Sunken ships often become artificial reefs where fish gather, and sharks follow.

en.clue: At risk of disappearing forever from the wild
en.fact: Many shark kinds are in trouble because they grow slowly and have few pups.

es.clue: Con esto ves; tienes dos en la cara

es.clue: Nadar bajo el agua con un tanque de aire

en.clue: Food from animals, like beef or chicken

en.clue: Hard white part inside a body that fossil hunters dig up
en.fact: Many meat-eating dinosaurs had hollow bones, like birds do, which kept them lighter.

en.clue: What fossil hunters do with shovels and brushes to find bones
en.fact: Paleontologists use tiny brushes and dental picks to uncover fossils without breaking them.

en.clue: Bony case that protects the brain
en.fact: A Triceratops skull could be longer than a grown-up is tall.

en.clue: Modern feathered animal with wings that is a living dinosaur
en.fact: Birds are living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered meat-eaters.

en.clue: Cloth that catches wind on a boat; Spinosaurus had a bony one
en.fact: Spinosaurus had a tall sail on its back and probably hunted fish in rivers.

en.clue: Dry ground, not the sea; where dinosaurs lived
en.fact: Sea reptiles like plesiosaurs lived at the same time, but they were not dinosaurs.

en.clue: Leafy plant with feathery fronds that grows in shady forests
en.fact: Ferns carpeted the ground in dinosaur times, long before grass spread.

en.clue: Body part a pterosaur flapped to fly
en.fact: Pterosaur wings were thin skin stretched from one very long finger.

en.clue: Types of food an animal usually eats
en.fact: Tooth shape tells scientists what a dinosaur ate: sharp for meat, flat for plants.

en.clue: The huge dark area beyond Earth's air, full of stars
en.fact: The asteroid that hit Earth about 66 million years ago was roughly six miles wide.

en.clue: Very large being in a fairy tale who says "fee-fi-fo-fum"
en.fact: Some long-necked dinosaurs may have been longer than a basketball court.

en.clue: Fluffy yellow baby that hatches from a hen's egg
en.fact: Scientists found that proteins in T. rex bone were most like a chicken's.

en.clue: Hard rock material that old bones turn into as fossils
en.fact: Fossil bones turn to stone as minerals slowly replace them over millions of years.

en.clue: Wet, sticky dirt that sticks to your boots
en.fact: A dinosaur footprint pressed in soft mud can turn into rock if it gets covered quickly.

en.clue: Sense you use your nose for
en.fact: T. rex had a very large smell center in its brain, so it probably smelled very well.

en.clue: Waterbird that says quack; one dinosaur group is named for its bill
en.fact: Duck-billed dinosaurs had hundreds of tiny teeth packed together for grinding plants.

en.clue: Flat green part of a plant that catches sunlight
en.fact: Many dinosaurs ate leaves from ginkgo trees, which still grow today.

en.clue: Moving at high speed, like a cheetah
en.fact: Gallimimus looked like an ostrich and probably ran about as fast as one.

en.clue: Chomp down with your teeth
en.fact: T. rex had one of the strongest bites of any land animal ever.

en.clue: Your backbone, or a sharp point on a cactus
en.fact: Spinosaurus means "spine lizard."

en.clue: Five wiggly digits on each of your feet
en.fact: Most meat-eating dinosaurs walked on three toes, leaving footprints like a bird's.

en.clue: Green blades that cover lawns and baseball fields
en.fact: Early dinosaurs had no grass to eat, because grasslands spread much later.

en.clue: Very, very small
en.fact: Some feathered dinosaurs were only about as big as a pigeon.

en.clue: Red-hot melted rock that pours from a volcano
en.fact: Huge lava eruptions in India happened around the time the dinosaurs died out.

en.clue: Small, fast, feathered hunter with a curved toe claw
en.fact: Real Velociraptors were about as big as turkeys and covered in feathers.

en.clue: Mountain that can erupt with lava and ash
en.fact: Volcanic ash sometimes buried dinosaurs quickly, which helped preserve their bones.

en.clue: Tree with fan-shaped leaves that has barely changed in millions of years
en.fact: Ginkgo trees grew in dinosaur times, so they are called living fossils.

en.clue: Thick, hot, wet forest full of vines
en.fact: Dinosaurs even lived in forests near the poles, where winters were dark.

en.clue: Typical weather of a place over many years
en.fact: Earth was much warmer in dinosaur times, with little or no ice at the poles.

en.clue: The process of getting bigger over time
en.fact: A teenage T. rex gained roughly five pounds every day.

en.clue: Digging tool with a flat blade and a long handle
en.fact: Fossil hunters use shovels for the top dirt, then switch to tiny tools near the bones.

en.clue: Tool for pounding nails; fossil hunters use small ones with chisels
en.fact: Paleontologists tap rock gently with small hammers to free fossils.

en.clue: Warm coat for cold weather; also a plaster wrap around a fossil
en.fact: Fossil hunters wrap bones in plaster jackets, like a cast on a broken arm.

en.clue: Dry, sandy region that gets very little rain
en.fact: Many famous dinosaur fossils come from deserts, where wind uncovers old bones.

en.clue: Deep valley with steep rock walls
en.fact: The rock layers in a canyon are like pages in a book about Earth's past.

en.clue: Large world circling a star, like Earth
en.fact: Earth is the only planet where dinosaur fossils have ever been found.

en.clue: A hard crash of one thing into another
en.fact: The asteroid's impact threw so much dust into the sky that it blocked sunlight.

en.clue: One of the five digits on your hand
en.fact: T. rex had only two fingers on each tiny arm.

en.clue: Giant flightless bird with long legs that runs very fast
en.fact: Ostriches sprint on two legs, much like many dinosaurs did.

en.clue: Insect with a hard shell-like back, like a ladybug
en.fact: Beetles lived alongside dinosaurs, and today there are more kinds of beetles than of any other animal group.

en.clue: How tall something is, from bottom to top
en.fact: Brachiosaurus stood about as tall as a four-story building.

en.clue: Dark bands, like a tiger or a zebra has
en.fact: Tiny pigment bits in fossils show that Sinosauropteryx had a striped tail.

en.clue: Natural coloring in skin, feathers, or fur
en.fact: Scientists found tiny pigment structures in fossil feathers and figured out some dinosaurs' colors.

en.clue: Machine that takes pictures of the inside of things
en.fact: CT scanners let scientists look inside fossil skulls without breaking them open.

en.clue: Building a home for eggs and sitting on them
en.fact: Oviraptor fossils have been found sitting on top of their eggs, like birds do.

en.clue: Tiny baby animal growing inside an egg
en.fact: Scientists have found fossil dinosaur eggs with embryos still curled up inside.

en.clue: To show off for others to admire
en.fact: Crests and horns may have been used to show off, like a peacock's tail.

en.clue: Light aircraft with no engine that floats on the wind
en.fact: Microraptor had feathers on its arms and legs and may have glided between trees.

en.clue: Spotted African animal with a very long neck
en.fact: Some long-necked dinosaurs had necks many times longer than a giraffe's.

en.clue: Fire-breathing flying creature from fairy tales
en.fact: Long ago, people who found dinosaur bones sometimes thought they were dragon bones.

en.clue: Colorful blooms on plants that bees visit
en.fact: The very first flowers appeared while dinosaurs were alive.

en.clue: Everything that happened in the past
en.fact: Dinosaurs ruled Earth for over 160 million years, far longer than humans have existed.

en.clue: A thousand thousands
en.fact: Dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

en.clue: A copy of the real thing, like a cast of a skull
en.fact: Most museum skeletons are copies, because real fossil bones are heavy and fragile.

en.clue: Game of pieces you fit together
en.fact: Fossil hunters often find bones scattered like puzzle pieces and fit them back together.

en.clue: Loud rumble that follows lightning
en.fact: Brontosaurus means "thunder lizard."

en.clue: Distance from one wingtip to the other
en.fact: Quetzalcoatlus had a wingspan about as wide as a small airplane.

en.clue: Tool that makes tiny things look much bigger
en.fact: Under a microscope, scientists can see growth rings in dinosaur bones that show how old it was.

en.clue: Machine with a screen and keyboard that runs programs and games
en.fact: Scientists use computers to test how fast a dinosaur could have run, based on its bones.

en.clue: Newborn animal that has just come out of its egg
en.fact: Even giant long-necked dinosaurs hatched from eggs much smaller than a beach ball.

en.clue: Animal that eats both plants and meat
en.fact: Scientists think some dinosaurs ate both plants and small animals.

en.clue: Big snouty reptile of African rivers, a living cousin of dinosaurs
en.fact: Crocodiles and birds are the closest living relatives of dinosaurs.

en.clue: Largest living land animal, with a trunk and tusks
en.fact: The biggest long-necked dinosaurs weighed many times more than an elephant.

en.clue: One of Earth's seven giant land areas
en.fact: Dinosaur fossils have been found on every continent, even Antarctica.

en.clue: Icy land at the bottom of the world
en.fact: Dinosaurs once lived there, when it was warmer and covered in forests.

en.clue: Feathered dinosaur whose name wrongly means "egg thief"
en.fact: Oviraptor was named by mistake; it was really guarding its own nest.

en.clue: Big meat-eater from the Jurassic, older cousin of T. rex
en.fact: Allosaurus lived about 80 million years before T. rex.

en.clue: Very long plant-eater whose name means "double beam"
en.fact: Diplodocus was longer than two school buses, but its head was small.

en.clue: Giant fish-eating dinosaur with a tall sail on its back
en.fact: Spinosaurus may have been even longer than T. rex.

en.clue: Plant-eater with spiky thumbs, one of the first dinosaurs named
en.fact: Iguanodon was named about 200 years ago, when people had only just begun finding dinosaurs.

en.clue: Long-necked sea reptile with four flippers; not a dinosaur
en.fact: Plesiosaurs flapped four flippers like wings to fly through the water.

en.clue: Giant sea lizard of the late dinosaur age
en.fact: Mosasaurs were giant sea reptiles related to today's snakes and lizards.

en.clue: Flying reptile with a pointed head crest and no teeth
en.fact: Pteranodon had no teeth, so it probably swallowed fish whole.

en.clue: Rock-hard fossil of animal droppings
en.fact: Coprolites show scientists what dinosaurs ate, sometimes even including bits of bone.

en.clue: Careful digging to uncover things buried long ago
en.fact: A big dinosaur dig can take many summers of careful work.

en.clue: Sand and mud that settle and pile up in layers
en.fact: Bones buried quickly in sediment have the best chance of becoming fossils.

en.clue: When a whole kind of animal disappears forever
en.fact: About three out of four kinds of living things died out when the dinosaurs did.

en.clue: Someone who lives through something dangerous
en.fact: Crocodiles, turtles, and birds all survived the event that ended the dinosaur age.

en.clue: The first of three periods in the age of dinosaurs
en.fact: The first dinosaurs appeared in the Triassic, about 230 million years ago.

en.clue: The middle period of the age of dinosaurs
en.fact: Long-necked giants like Diplodocus lived in the Jurassic, which is named after the Jura Mountains.

es.clue: Persona con corona que gobierna un reino
es.fact: El nombre Tyrannosaurus rex significa "rey de los lagartos tiranos".

es.clue: Los alimentos que come normalmente un animal
es.fact: La forma de los dientes muestra si un dinosaurio comía carne o plantas.

es.clue: Pie y pierna de un animal, como la de un perro
es.fact: Los dinosaurios caminaban con las patas debajo del cuerpo, no abiertas a los lados como un lagarto.

es.clue: Parte del cuerpo con la que vuela un ave
es.fact: Las alas de los pterosaurios eran de piel delgada, estirada desde un dedo larguísimo.

es.clue: Moverse por el aire con alas
es.fact: Los pterosaurios volaban sobre los dinosaurios, aunque no eran dinosaurios.

es.clue: Tierra mojada y pegajosa que se te pega en los zapatos
es.fact: Una huella en barro blando puede volverse roca si algo la cubre rápido.

es.clue: Material duro de las montañas, en el que se forman los fósiles
es.fact: Los fósiles se forman en capas de roca que antes fueron arena y lodo.

es.clue: Estrella que da luz y calor a la Tierra
es.fact: La luz del Sol tarda unos ocho minutos en llegar a la Tierra.

es.clue: Roca derretida y roja que sale de un volcán
es.fact: Enormes erupciones de lava en la India ocurrieron más o menos cuando se extinguieron los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Ave de granja que se sirve frita o al horno
es.fact: Los pollos son aves, y las aves son dinosaurios vivos.

es.clue: Ave de pico plano que nada en lagunas y dice cuac
es.fact: Los hadrosaurios, llamados dinosaurios de pico de pato, eran herbívoros.

es.clue: Cada una de las cinco partes móviles de tu mano
es.fact: El T. rex tenía solo dos dedos en cada brazo diminuto.

es.clue: Parte del cuerpo entre el hombro y la mano
es.fact: Los brazos del T. rex eran cortos, pero tenían huesos gruesos y mucho músculo.

es.clue: Tela grande que atrapa el viento en un barco
es.fact: El espinosaurio tenía una gran vela en la espalda y probablemente cazaba peces en los ríos.

es.clue: Parte plana y verde de una planta que atrapa la luz
es.fact: Los dinosaurios de cuello largo estiraban el cuello para alcanzar las hojas más altas de los árboles.

es.clue: Hierba verde y corta que cubre las canchas
es.fact: Los primeros dinosaurios no tenían pasto para comer, porque los pastizales aparecieron mucho después.

es.clue: Bosque caliente y húmedo, lleno de plantas y lianas
es.fact: Había dinosaurios en bosques cerca de los polos, donde los inviernos eran oscuros.

es.clue: Herramienta de hoja plana para cavar
es.fact: Los cazadores de fósiles usan palas para la tierra de arriba y pinceles pequeños cerca de los huesos.

es.clue: Polvo blanco que, mojado, se endurece y protege un brazo roto
es.fact: Los cazadores de fósiles envuelven los huesos en yeso para llevarlos sin romperlos.

es.clue: Gran cantidad de agua dulce rodeada de tierra
es.fact: Muchos fósiles de dinosaurio aparecen donde antes había lagos y ríos, porque el lodo cubría los huesos.

es.clue: Planta grande con tronco, ramas y hojas
es.fact: Los árboles de ginkgo crecían en tiempos de los dinosaurios y todavía existen.

es.clue: Parte colorida de una planta que visitan las abejas
es.fact: Las primeras flores aparecieron cuando todavía vivían los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Cuántos años tiene alguien o algo
es.fact: Los T. rex más viejos que se conocen tenían unos 28 años.

es.clue: Tierra muy fina y seca que flota en el aire
es.fact: El polvo que levantó el asteroide tapó la luz del Sol durante mucho tiempo.

es.clue: Agua congelada, dura y fría
es.fact: Cuando vivían los dinosaurios casi no había hielo en los polos, porque el clima era más cálido.

es.clue: Máquina que se mueve y trabaja sola
es.fact: Algunos museos tienen dinosaurios robot que se mueven y hacen sonidos.

es.clue: Satélite natural que vemos brillar de noche
es.fact: Los cráteres de la Luna se formaron por choques de asteroides, como el que acabó con los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Pedazo de tierra rodeado de agua por todos lados
es.fact: Europasaurus, un dinosaurio de cuello largo, vivió en una isla y era pequeño.

es.clue: Pieza dura de la boca que sirve para masticar
es.fact: Algunos dientes de T. rex eran tan largos como un plátano.

es.clue: Planta de hojas plumosas que crece en lugares sombríos
es.fact: Los helechos cubrían el suelo en tiempos de los dinosaurios, mucho antes que el pasto.

es.clue: Trozo duro de roca que puedes levantar del suelo
es.fact: Los huesos de dinosaurio se vuelven piedra cuando los minerales los reemplazan durante millones de años.

es.clue: El enorme vacío oscuro más allá del aire de la Tierra
es.fact: El asteroide que chocó con la Tierra hace unos 66 millones de años medía unos diez kilómetros.

es.clue: Hueso duro que protege el cerebro
es.fact: El cráneo de un tricerátops podía medir más que un adulto de alto.

es.clue: Criatura de cuentos que vuela y echa fuego
es.fact: Hace mucho, quienes encontraban huesos de dinosaurio a veces creían que eran de dragón.

es.clue: Ave de granja que pone huevos para el desayuno
es.fact: Los científicos vieron que las proteínas del T. rex se parecían mucho a las de una gallina.

es.clue: Nuestro planeta, el tercero desde el Sol
es.fact: La Tierra tiene unos 4,500 millones de años, y los dinosaurios llegaron mucho después.

es.clue: Apretón fuerte que das con los dientes
es.fact: La mordida del T. rex era de las más fuertes de cualquier animal terrestre.

es.clue: Herramienta con cerdas para pintar o limpiar con suavidad
es.fact: Los paleontólogos limpian los fósiles con pinceles pequeños para no romperlos.

es.clue: Montaña que puede echar lava y ceniza
es.fact: Un volcán puede lanzar ceniza a muchos kilómetros de altura.

es.clue: Choque fuerte de un objeto contra otro
es.fact: El asteroide que chocó con la Tierra dejó un cráter de unos 180 kilómetros de ancho.

es.clue: Bola de hielo y polvo con una cola brillante en el espacio
es.fact: Los cometas y los asteroides son sobras de cuando se formó el Sistema Solar.

es.clue: Animal africano de manchas y cuello larguísimo
es.fact: Algunos dinosaurios de cuello largo tenían un cuello mucho más largo que el de una jirafa.

es.clue: Dinosaurio pequeño y veloz con una garra curva en el pie
es.fact: Los velociraptores de verdad eran del tamaño de un pavo y tenían plumas.

es.clue: Bebé muy pequeño que crece dentro del huevo
es.fact: Se han encontrado huevos fósiles de dinosaurio con embriones enroscados adentro.

es.clue: Hacerse más grande con el paso del tiempo
es.fact: Un T. rex adolescente aumentaba unos dos kilos al día.

es.clue: Qué tan alto es algo, de abajo hacia arriba
es.fact: Un braquiosaurio era tan alto como un edificio de cuatro pisos.

es.clue: Máquina que toma imágenes del interior de las cosas
es.fact: Con escáneres, los científicos pueden ver dentro de un cráneo fósil sin romperlo.

es.clue: Volar sin batir las alas, dejándose llevar por el aire
es.fact: El microraptor tenía plumas en brazos y piernas, y quizá planeaba entre los árboles.

es.clue: Mil veces mil
es.fact: Los dinosaurios desaparecieron hace unos 66 millones de años.

es.clue: Copia de algo real, como el molde de un cráneo
es.fact: Muchos esqueletos de los museos son copias, porque los huesos de verdad son pesados y frágiles.

es.clue: Ruido fuerte y grave que se oye después del rayo
es.fact: Brontosaurio significa "lagarto del trueno".

es.clue: Material duro natural, como el cuarzo, que se forma en las rocas
es.fact: Un hueso se vuelve fósil cuando los minerales lo llenan y lo endurecen.

es.clue: Terreno con muchísimos árboles
es.fact: Los bosques de la época de los dinosaurios tenían coníferas, helechos y plantas parecidas a palmeras.

es.clue: Terreno bajo cubierto de agua poco profunda y lodo
es.fact: Muchos fósiles se formaron en pantanos, donde el lodo cubría rápido los huesos.

es.clue: Forma en que un animal se protege de los ataques
es.fact: El estegosaurio se defendía golpeando con su cola llena de púas.

es.clue: Moverse con los pies, paso a paso
es.fact: Los científicos calculan qué tan rápido caminaba un dinosaurio midiendo la distancia entre sus huellas.

es.clue: Moverse a pie muy rápido, más que al caminar
es.fact: Gallimimus se parecía a un avestruz y probablemente corría igual de rápido.

es.clue: Lo que escuchas con tus oídos
es.fact: Algunos dinosaurios con cresta quizá hacían sonidos graves al soplar por ella.

es.clue: Polvo gris que queda de lo quemado y sale de los volcanes
es.fact: La ceniza volcánica enterró a algunos animales rápido y ayudó a conservarlos.

es.clue: Roca negra que se quema, hecha de plantas antiguas
es.fact: El carbón se formó con plantas enterradas hace cientos de millones de años.

es.clue: Región seca y arenosa donde casi no llueve
es.fact: Muchos fósiles famosos de dinosaurio vienen de desiertos, donde el viento deja al descubierto huesos antiguos.

es.clue: Ave enorme que no vuela, de patas largas, y corre muy rápido
es.fact: El avestruz es el ave viva más grande, y es pariente de los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Reptil grande de hocico largo y mandíbulas fuertes, pariente de los dinosaurios
es.fact: Los cocodrilos y las aves son los parientes vivos más cercanos de los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Aparato que hace ver enormes las cosas diminutas
es.fact: Con un microscopio, los científicos ven cómo creció un hueso de dinosaurio, como los anillos de un árbol.

es.clue: Máquina con pantalla y teclado donde haces tareas y juegas
es.fact: Los científicos usan computadoras para calcular qué tan rápido corría un dinosaurio según sus huesos.

es.clue: Color natural de la piel, las plumas o el pelo
es.fact: Se hallaron restos diminutos de pigmento en plumas fósiles y así se descubrieron los colores de algunos dinosaurios.

es.clue: Seguir con vida después de un peligro
es.fact: Cocodrilos, tortugas y aves sobrevivieron al suceso que acabó con los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Cuando toda una clase de animales desaparece para siempre
es.fact: Cuando murieron los dinosaurios, desapareció cerca de tres de cada cuatro tipos de seres vivos.

es.clue: El periodo medio de la era de los dinosaurios
es.fact: Muchos gigantes de cuello largo vivieron en el Jurásico, que lleva el nombre de las montañas del Jura.

es.clue: El primer periodo de la era de los dinosaurios
es.fact: Los primeros dinosaurios aparecieron en el Triásico, hace unos 230 millones de años.

es.clue: Arena y lodo que se asientan y forman capas
es.fact: Los huesos cubiertos rápido por sedimento tienen más posibilidades de volverse fósiles.

es.clue: Distancia de la punta de un ala a la otra
es.fact: El Quetzalcoatlus tenía una envergadura tan ancha como la de un avión pequeño.

es.clue: Hueso que mueves al abrir y cerrar la boca
es.fact: Algunos dinosaurios de pico de pato tenían cientos de dientes en las mandíbulas.

es.clue: Gran carnívoro del Jurásico, más antiguo que el T. rex
es.fact: El alosaurio vivió unos 80 millones de años antes que el T. rex.

es.clue: Herbívoro larguísimo cuyo nombre significa "doble viga"
es.fact: Medía más que dos autobuses escolares, pero tenía la cabeza pequeña.

es.clue: Herbívoro con pulgares en forma de púa, de los primeros dinosaurios nombrados
es.fact: Fue uno de los primeros dinosaurios con nombre, hace unos 200 años.

es.clue: Gran reptil marino del Cretácico, pariente de serpientes y lagartos
es.fact: Los mosasaurios no eran dinosaurios: eran reptiles marinos gigantes.

es.clue: Dinosaurio con plumas cuyo nombre significa por error "ladrón de huevos"
es.fact: Lo llamaron así por error: en realidad cuidaba sus propios huevos.

es.clue: Fósil duro como piedra de excremento de animal
es.fact: Los coprolitos muestran qué comían los dinosaurios, a veces con pedacitos de hueso.

es.clue: Cavar con cuidado para sacar cosas enterradas hace mucho
es.fact: Una excavación grande de dinosaurios puede tardar muchos veranos de trabajo cuidadoso.

es.clue: Una de las enormes masas de tierra del planeta
es.fact: Se han encontrado fósiles de dinosaurio en todos los continentes, hasta en la Antártida.

es.clue: Tierra helada en el extremo sur del planeta
es.fact: Hubo dinosaurios allí cuando era más cálida y tenía bosques.

es.clue: Animal con pelo que alimenta a sus crías con leche
es.fact: Los primeros mamíferos eran pequeños y vivían junto a los dinosaurios.

es.clue: Árbol como el pino, con hojas de aguja y piñas
es.fact: Los dinosaurios de cuello largo probablemente comían coníferas, parientes de los pinos de hoy.
